content.title: About
content.content: Pita is a flat bread made from wheat flour, typical of Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines. The dough is rolled into round discs and baked at high temperature, causing a pocket to form in the centre as steam expands.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pita can be soft or slightly crisp depending on baking time.
Traditionally it is served with hummus, kebab, falafel and other Middle Eastern dishes.
Bread shapes similar to modern pita are mentioned in ancient Egyptian texts.
The pocket inside pita is created by rapid evaporation of moisture from the dough during baking.
In some regions pita is called “Arabic bread” or “lavash”.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Pita provides a quick source of energy thanks to its high content of complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other breads, traditional pita contains little fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour used for pita is rich in thiamine, niacin and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Pita provides iron, magnesium and phosphorus, supporting blood health and bone function.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Its soft texture and small size make pita easy to eat quickly and digest.

items.title: Gluten intolerance
items.content: Pita contains gluten, so people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid it.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because its carbohydrates are absorbed quickly, pita should be eaten in moderation, especially by people with diabetes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some commercially prepared pitas contain added salt; those with hypertension should choose low‑salt versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut pita along the side to open a “pocket” and fill it with meat, vegetables, sauces or salads. It can also be used as a sandwich base, served alongside soups, or as a side for grilled dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep pita in an airtight bag at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, place it in a paper bag in the refrigerator to retain softness without becoming soggy. Freeze in a plastic bag for up to 3 months; reheat in the oven or microwave before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Pinto beans are a variety of dry legume popular in Mexican and South American cuisines. Brown rice is a whole‑grain rice that retains its bran and germ, making it more nutritious than white rice. Together they provide a balanced mix of protein, complex carbohydrates, and fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “pinto” comes from the Spanish word for “painted,” referring to the bean’s mottled skin.
Brown rice retains more B‑vitamins and minerals than white rice because the outer layers are kept intact.
Combining beans and rice supplies all essential amino acids, creating a complete plant‑based protein source.
Pinto beans are rich in antioxidants, including phenolic compounds that may support heart health.
When stored properly (dry, cool place) beans can last up to a year, and rice up to six months.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Plant‑based protein source
items.content: The bean‑rice combo provides about 15‑20 g of protein per serving, valuable for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: Pinto beans are a good source of iron, while brown rice supplies magnesium, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Both foods raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phenolics in beans and vitamin E in rice help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Beans and whole grains contain phytates that can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and sprouting lower their levels.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Legumes can cause flatulence; gradual introduction and thorough rinsing help mitigate this.

items.title: Arsenic content in rice
items.content: Brown rice may contain trace amounts of inorganic arsenic; varying grain sources is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak pinto beans for at least 6 hours, then simmer until tender (about 1‑1.5 h). Rinse brown rice and cook in a 1:2.5 water ratio for 40‑45 minutes. Combine them in pilafs, soups, salads, or use as a base for vegetarian burgers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place – up to 12 months. Keep brown rice in a sealed container, preferably in the refrigerator, to prevent oil oxidation; shelf life is 6‑12 months.

rice-brown-with-cheese-and-or-cream-base.title: Brown Rice with Cheese and/or Cream Based Sauce, NS as to Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain rice that retains the bran and germ. Combined with a cheese or cream‑based sauce it creates a nutritious dish commonly used in various cuisines. Fat content is listed as NS (not specified).

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains more nutrients than white rice because the bran layer is kept intact.
Cheese sauce can be made from a variety of cheeses such as cheddar, parmesan, or processed cheese.
Cream sauce is often prepared with cream, butter, and seasonings, giving a smooth, rich flavor.
In some cultures brown rice with cheese or cream sauce is served as a side to meat dishes.
When stored properly, brown rice can stay fresh for up to a year.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: The bran in brown rice provides a good amount of dietary fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Brown rice releases glucose slowly, helping maintain steady energy levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice supplies thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Brown rice offers magnesium, phosphorus, and iron, beneficial for muscles and bones.

items.title: Protein from cheese
items.content: Cheese sauce adds complete protein and calcium, supporting bone health.

items.title: High fat content in sauce
items.content: Cream and cheese sauces can be calorie‑dense and contain saturated fats; moderation is advised.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort from cheese and cream.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cheese sauces often contain significant salt; consider this if you limit sodium intake.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have allergic reactions to dairy ingredients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cooked brown rice topped with hot cheese or cream sauce. Add vegetables, herbs, or spices to taste. The dish works well as a side to meat or fish, or as a vegetarian main course.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry brown rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice and sauce should be cooled and refrigerated, lasting 3‑4 days. Sauce can be frozen for up to 2 months.

rice-white-with-lentils-no-added-fat.title: White Rice with Lentils, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: White rice with lentils, no added fat is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of boiled white rice and red lentils prepared without oil or other fats. It provides a blend of easily digestible carbohydrates and plant protein, along with fiber and micronutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The rice‑lentil combination is a staple in Middle Eastern and Mediterranean cuisines.
Lentils contain three times more protein than most cereal grains.
White rice is quickly absorbed, while lentils slow the rise of blood sugar, making the dish more balanced.
The product contains no added fats, suitable for low‑calorie diets.
Cooking without oil preserves the natural flavors of the ingredients.

items.title: Plant‑based protein source
items.content: Lentils provide about 9 g of protein per 100 g of product, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: The rice‑lentil mix delivers roughly 5 g of fiber, aiding digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Absence of added fats makes the dish suitable for calorie‑restricted eating plans.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: Lentils are a good source of iron and folic acid, important for blood formation and nervous system health.

items.title: Supports blood‑sugar stability
items.content: Fiber and slowly digestible carbs help keep glucose levels steady after meals.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lentils.

items.title: High glycemic index of rice
items.content: White rice has a high GI, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Lentils contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The dish can be enjoyed as a standalone meal or added to salads, soups, and vegetable stews. It reheats well in the microwave or on the stovetop; feel free to season with herbs, spices, or a squeeze of lemon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. When frozen, keep for up to 3 months. Discard if you notice off‑odors, discoloration, or mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Wild pig refers to the meat of wild boars that roam forested regions of Europe and Asia. It has a richer, slightly sweet flavor and a firmer texture compared with domestic pork. Wild pig is commonly used in traditional dishes such as stews, sausages, and smoked specialties.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wild pig meat contains less fat but more protein than domestic pork.
Boars adapt quickly to different habitats, giving the meat a varied taste depending on their diet.
In several cultures wild pig is considered a delicacy and is featured in festive meals.
Boars can weigh up to 200 kg, and their meat is noted for a higher iron content.
Traditionally the meat is smoked over wood smoke, imparting a distinctive aroma.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Wild pig provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High iron content
items.content: The iron in wild pig is readily absorbed and helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Compared with domestic pork, wild pig contains less saturated fat, making it a better option for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It is a good source of B12, B6 and niacin, which support the nervous system and metabolism.

items.title: Essential minerals
items.content: Wild pig supplies zinc, selenium and phosphorus, important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Parasite risk
items.content: Wild boar can carry trichinella and other parasites; the meat must be thoroughly cooked.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to wild game meat.

items.title: High sodium in smoked products
items.content: Smoked wild pig products often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Cooking challenges
items.content: If not properly marinated or cooked at the right temperature, the meat can become tough.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The meat is usually marinated with herbs and spices, then braised, roasted, or smoked. Wild pig works well in stews, sausages, roasts, and kebabs. Marinating for at least 4–6 hours helps tenderize the fibers before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh wild pig in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for no more than 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C; it keeps quality for up to 6 months. Before cooking, check for off‑odors or discoloration.
